prompt.context: Your client is Putter, a company that publishes romance novels that they sell to bookstores. Typically, Putter reimburses its customers at the end of the year for any unsold inventory. Now, one of Putter's customers, a retail bookstore, has come to it with an offer for a deal. In return for a 10% discount on wholesale prices, the bookstore will no longer send back any books at the end of the year.
prompt.question: Should Putter do the deal?

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to produce a book?
clarifying_info.a: It costs Putter $5 on average to make a single book.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current wholesale price?
clarifying_info.a: Putter previously sold books to the bookstore at $10 per book.

clarifying_info.q: What is the MSRP or retail price?
clarifying_info.a: MSRP is not relevant to this analysis; Putter's clients must sell at the price Putter dictates, no cheaper.

clarifying_info.q: What is the salvage value of unsold/returned books?
clarifying_info.a: Putter's salvage value for unsold books is $0.

clarifying_info.q: How many books did the bookstore order last year?
clarifying_info.a: In 2008, Putter sold 10,000 books to this bookstore.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of books were returned last year?
clarifying_info.a: In 2008, the retail bookstore sent back 20% of its books.

clarifying_info.q: How many books would the bookstore order under the new deal?
clarifying_info.a: The projected order under the new deal is 7,500 books.

clarifying_info.q: What are the market trends for romance novels?
clarifying_info.a: Romance novel sales have been flat for a decade and are expected to remain so in the coming years.

framework: Margin / Profitability analysis: compare pre- and post-deal profit using cost, price, volume, and returns
Cash flow impact: compare upfront cash received before vs. after the deal
Market share impact: compare net books sold (reaching consumers) before vs. after the deal

Strategic / qualitative considerations: opportunities (reduced complexity, goodwill, new distribution) and threats (contagion to other clients, weaker channel relationship, lower cash flow in a tough economy)

questions.prompt: Does this deal make sense on a profit basis? Calculate pre- and post-deal profit for Putter.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that pre-deal, 20% of 10,000 books (2,000 books) are returned at cost $5 each with no salvage, so net units sold = 8,000. Post-deal, bookstore orders 7,500 with no returns. Price drops 10% from $10 to $9. Strong candidates note salvage value = 0 so returns are a pure cost. Profit should be identical at $30,000 in both scenarios.

math.setup: Pre-deal: 10,000 books ordered; 20% returned = 2,000 returned; 8,000 net sold. Wholesale price = $10; cost = $5; salvage = $0. Post-deal: 7,500 books ordered; 0 returned. New wholesale price = $10 * (1 - 10%) = $9; cost = $5.
steps: Pre-deal profit = (net units sold) * (price - cost) - (returned units) * cost = 8,000 * (10 - 5) - 2,000 * 5 = 40,000 - 10,000 = $30,000
math.answer: Pre-deal profit = $30,000; Post-deal profit = $30,000. Profit is identical.

questions.prompt: What is the cash flow impact of the deal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare upfront cash received. Pre-deal, Putter receives payment on all 10,000 books shipped; some cash is returned at year-end when books come back. Post-deal, Putter collects only on 7,500 books at the lower price. The deal significantly reduces upfront cash received, which is especially problematic in a difficult economic environment.

math.setup: Pre-deal: Putter ships 10,000 books at $10 each upfront. Post-deal: Putter ships 7,500 books at $9 each upfront.
math.answer: Upfront cash declines from $100,000 to $67,500, a reduction of $32,500 (~33% lower).

questions.prompt: What is the market share impact?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that net units actually reaching consumers drops from 8,000 to 7,500 under the new deal, meaning Putter's presence on shelves shrinks even though books are guaranteed to sell through.

math.setup: Pre-deal net books sold = 10,000 - 2,000 returns = 8,000. Post-deal net books sold = 7,500 (no returns).
steps: Pre-deal market share proxy: 8,000 books in market
Post-deal market share proxy: 7,500 books in market
Decline = 500 fewer books, roughly 6.25% less presence
math.answer: Market share (books in consumers' hands) declines from 8,000 to 7,500.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the strategic opportunities and threats of accepting this deal?

categories.name: Opportunities
ideas: Reduction in operational complexity (no returns processing)
Goodwill from meeting a customer/channel request
Opens a new business model that may lead to additional distribution channels
Bookstore has stronger incentive to sell through if they bear inventory risk

categories.name: Threats
ideas: Lower upfront cash flow — problematic in a difficult economic environment
Fewer net units sold reduces market presence and brand awareness
May set a precedent: other bookstores could demand the same discount (first of many, not an isolated case)
Supplying the bookstore with fewer books may make Putter seem less important as a partner
Relationship risk if Putter declines while other publishers accept similar deals

recommendation: The deal does not appear attractive on a financial or strategic basis.
Expected profitability is identical ($30,000) but upfront cash flow drops ~33% ($100K to $67.5K) and net market share declines from 8,000 to 7,500 units.
Recommendation is NOT to accept the deal in its current form.
risks: By declining, Putter risks alienating the bookstore if other publishers shift to this business model.
If this becomes an industry norm, Putter may be forced to accept worse terms later with less negotiating leverage.
next_steps: Consider whether a differentiated pricing model could make sense for specific title types — e.g., guaranteed no-return terms at a smaller discount for blockbuster titles vs. high-volume genre titles.
Monitor competitor responses to understand whether this deal type is becoming a market standard.
Analyze whether the cash flow shortfall ($32,500) can be offset through cost reductions or financing.
